conceptTag: A tech company with a pile of cash
readerTitle: Your software company has $30M in the bank. Now what?
caseNote: 가상 사례 (급여 소프트웨어 회사, 포장재 제조사) · 모든 수치는 설명용
insight: 쌓인 현금은 '어디에 쓸까'가 아니라 '어떤 쓰임이 같은 기준선을 넘는가'로 판단하고, 넘는 곳이 없으면 돌려주는 것도 정답이다.
misconception: 현금이 많으면 뭐라도 해야 한다. 전략적인 인수라면 수익률이 낮아도 괜찮다.

sources.text: 기업재무의 표준 개념 (허들 레이트, 재투자·환원·인수 선택)

factChecks.note: 모든 수치는 설명용 가상 수치입니다. 소프트웨어 회사: 현금 $30M − 안전 버퍼 $5M = $25M. AI 추가 기능 $6M + 유럽 영업팀 $4M = $10M, 남는 돈 $25M − $10M = $15M. 인수: 연 이익 $1.2M ÷ $20M = 6%.
포장재 제조사: 여유 현금 $3M − 자동화 라인 $1.8M = $1.2M. 건물 매입 $2.5M로 절약되는 임차료 연 $175k ÷ $2.5M = 7%, 허들 10%보다 낮음. 은행 이자율은 특정 수치를 쓰지 않고 '허들보다 낮을 가능성이 크다'고만 적었습니다.

cards.title: Your software company has $30M in the bank. Now what?
body: A payroll software company has had three strong years. The finance lead puts one number on the board slide: **$30M in cash**, and about $8M more coming each year.
Someone says, "It's just sitting there." Within ten minutes, three people have three different plans for it.

image.label: Board table with a large stack of cash and three people pointing different ways
image.brief: 3D 클레이 스타일. 회의 테이블 가운데 큰 현금 더미, 둘러앉은 세 사람이 각각 다른 방향(전구, 지구본, 작은 건물)을 가리킴. 실제 기업 로고나 상표 없음.

cards.title: What should the board do first?
body: The ideas on the table: build a new product, expand abroad, or buy a smaller rival. One director wants to pay it all out to shareholders instead.

options.text: Buy the rival now, before someone else does
options.feedback: Speed feels like strategy, but you'd commit the biggest sum before comparing it with anything else.

options.text: Set one hurdle rate and test every idea against it, including paying cash out
options.feedback: This puts **hurdle rates** and **reinvest, return or acquire** to work together. Every use of cash competes on the same terms.

options.text: Pay it all out. Owners can invest it themselves
options.feedback: Returning cash is a real option, but doing it first skips projects that might earn far more inside the business.

cards.title: Four claims on the same $30M.
body: The team keeps $5M as a buffer for a bad year. That leaves **$25M** to allocate.

cards.title: Which ideas clear 12%?
body: The board sets a **12% hurdle rate**: the return owners could reasonably expect elsewhere for similar risk.
Two ideas clear it. The acquisition, the biggest and most exciting, falls well short.

cards.title: The CEO pushes back on the acquisition.
body: "It's strategic," the CEO says. "Their customers could buy our other products, and we'd cut duplicate costs."

options.text: Approve it. Strategic value is hard to measure
options.feedback: "Strategic" can become a way to skip the **hurdle rate**. You'd pay $20M for 6% unless the benefits are real.

options.text: Ask for a realistic case with those savings and sales, then test it against 12%
options.feedback: The **hurdle rate** stays the same; only the honest numbers change. If the deal clears 12% with believable savings, buying beats building.
Caution is fair, but a blanket rule removes acquiring from your choices. Some deals do clear the bar.

cards.title: $15M with nowhere good to go.
body: Fund the AI add-on and the sales team, and $15M remains. This is where **reinvest, return or acquire** matters most.

Holding it earns bank interest, likely well below 12%. Returning it through dividends or buybacks lets owners put it to better use. Keeping some for a future deal is reasonable, but only with a plan and a deadline.

image.label: Three doors labeled Reinvest, Return and Acquire
image.brief: 문 세 개가 나란히 있고 각각 "Reinvest", "Return", "Acquire" 라벨. 현금 더미가 문 앞에 놓여 있고, "Reinvest" 문은 살짝 열려 있으며 "Return" 문으로 향하는 화살표. 로고 없음.

cards.title: The returns are estimates, not facts.
body: The 25% and 15% came from the people who want the money. Project owners tend to be optimistic, so ask how each estimate was built.
Risk differs too. A new product is riskier than more sales staff for a product that already sells. Riskier bets often deserve a **higher hurdle**, not the same one.
And keep the buffer. Cash you can't reach in a downturn is worth less than it looks.

cards.title: Now it's a packaging factory.
body: A family-owned packaging maker has $3M of spare cash after its buffer. Hurdle rate: 10%.
A second automated line costs $1.8M and should return about 18%. Buying the building it rents costs $2.5M and saves $175k a year in rent, about 7%.

options.text: Fund the line, then pay the remaining $1.2M out to the owners
options.feedback: The line clears the **hurdle rate**, the building doesn't, and returning the rest is the **return** option doing its job.

options.text: Buy the building. Owning feels safer than renting
options.feedback: You gain control of your site but lock $2.5M into a 7% return, below what the owners need.

options.text: Keep all $3M in the bank until a big opportunity appears
options.feedback: You stay flexible, but you skip an 18% project and leave cash earning less than the hurdle.

cards.title: A pile of cash is a list of choices, not a problem to spend away.
body: Today you used two ideas. **Hurdle rates** told you which projects earn their keep. **Reinvest, return or acquire** told you what to do with the rest, including giving it back.
**Try it today:** list every place your spare cash could go. Write an honest return next to each, then draw a line at your hurdle rate.
